questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the glans penis for 10 days. The base is clean, indurated and non-tender. Inguinal lymph nodes are enlarged, firm and non-tender. Dark-field microscopy shows motile spirochetes. Which of the following statements about this condition is FALSE?
opts: The causative organism is a microaerophilic spirochete
RPR can be negative in early primary syphilis
Treatment of choice is benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU single dose
Condylomata lata are a feature of this stage
questions.exp: Condylomata lata are moist, flat-topped papules seen in secondary syphilis, not primary syphilis. Primary syphilis presents with chancre (painless, indurated ulcer) and regional lymphadenopathy. RPR may be negative early in primary syphilis (prozone phenomenon or pre-seroconversion). Treatment is benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM single dose.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with a crusted plaque with central scarring and peripheral pustules on his forearm for 3 months. Culture on Sabouraud's dextrose agar grows a slow-growing colony with alternate bands of dark and light coloration. Lactophenol cotton blue preparation shows thick-walled, muriform (sclerotic) cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) presents with warty/verrucous plaques on extremities, often in agricultural workers. The hallmark is muriform (sclerotic/Medlar) bodies in tissue — thick-walled, dark brown cells with transverse septa. Causative organisms include Fonsecaea pedrosoi and Cladophialophora carrionii. Sporotrichosis causes sporotrichoid lymphocutaneous pattern; mycetoma shows grains in sinuses.

questions.q: A 7-year-old child presents with honey-crusted vesicles and erosions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain of crust shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which toxin is responsible for the superficial cleavage seen in bullous impetigo?
opts: Exfoliative toxin A and B targeting desmoglein 1
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) are caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (ETA/ETB) produced by Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. These toxins are serine proteases that specifically cleave desmoglein 1, causing intraepidermal split in the granular layer. Panton-Valentine leukocidin is associated with necrotising skin infections. Desmoglein 3 is targeted in pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man with a 20-year history of leprosy presents with sudden onset of painful red nodular lesions on his face and extremities, high fever (39.5°C), and orchitis. His previous leprosy type was lepromatous. Slit-skin smear shows BI of 4+. What is the FIRST-LINE treatment for his acute reaction?
questions.exp: This is Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL), a Type 2 lepra reaction seen in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. Thalidomide is the drug of choice for ENL in males (contraindicated in women of childbearing age due to teratogenicity). It works by inhibiting TNF-alpha and modulating immune response. Prednisolone is used when thalidomide is contraindicated (women). Clofazimine (300 mg/day) is used for chronic recurrent ENL. MDT must be continued throughout.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with tense blisters on an urticarial base on the trunk and flexures for 6 weeks. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the dermoepidermal junction. Indirect IMF shows antibodies binding to the roof of salt-split skin. What is the target antigen?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune blistering disorder. Antibodies target BP180 (BPAG2, type XVII collagen) and BP230 (BPAG1), which are components of hemidesmosomes. On salt-split skin, antibodies bind the roof (epidermal side), distinguishing it from EBA (dermal side — type VII collagen). Desmoglein 1 and 3 are targets in pemphigus. Laminin-332 is targeted in mucous membrane pemphigoid.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with photosensitive malar rash, oral ulcers, joint pain, and proteinuria. ANA is positive at 1:640, anti-dsDNA strongly positive, and complement C3 and C4 are low. Which of the following skin findings is MOST specific for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)?
questions.exp: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) plaques with follicular plugging, central scarring, and peripheral hyperpigmentation are specific features of lupus (both DLE and SLE). Periungual telangiectasias with ragged cuticles and Gottron's papules are features of dermatomyositis. Calcinosis cutis is seen in systemic sclerosis and dermatomyositis. The malar/butterfly rash of SLE is characteristically photosensitive and spares the nasolabial folds.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders, central ulceration, and telangiectasias on the nose for 8 months. He has a history of significant sun exposure. Dermoscopy shows arborising vessels and blue-grey ovoid nests. What is the MOST common histological subtype of this condition?
questions.exp: This is basal cell carcinoma (BCC), the most common malignant skin tumour. The nodular subtype is the most common (60–80%), presenting as the classic pearly papule with rolled borders, telangiectasias, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer) on sun-exposed areas of face. Dermoscopy shows arborising vessels, spoke-wheel areas, and blue-grey ovoid nests. Morpheaform is the most aggressive subtype with highest recurrence rate. Superficial BCC appears as erythematous patches on trunk.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with depigmented macules on her face and hands that fluoresce bright yellow-green under Wood's lamp. Lesional skin biopsy shows absence of melanocytes on DOPA stain. Which of the following drugs has shown BEST evidence for repigmentation in this condition?
questions.exp: This is vitiligo. Narrowband UVB (NB-UVB, 311 nm) is currently the gold standard phototherapy for generalised vitiligo, offering the best repigmentation rates with a good safety profile. It stimulates melanocyte proliferation, migration from hair follicle reservoirs, and modulates the immune response. Oral dexamethasone minipulse is useful for active/spreading vitiligo. Tacrolimus is effective for face and body vitiligo as monotherapy but is less effective than NB-UVB overall. Combination NB-UVB with tacrolimus is synergistic.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a 3-week history of dysuria and urethral discharge. He also complains of painful red eyes and arthritis affecting the knees and ankles. There is no history of similar symptoms before. He is HIV negative. Which investigation should be performed FIRST?
opts: Urethral swab for NAAT for Chlamydia trachomatis
questions.exp: This clinical triad of urethritis, conjunctivitis, and arthritis (can't see, can't pee, can't climb a tree) is Reactive Arthritis (formerly Reiter's syndrome). Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common precipitating STI. First investigation is urethral NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) for Chlamydia. HLA-B27 is associated in ~75% but is not a first-line diagnostic test. Synovial fluid shows sterile inflammatory arthritis. Treating the underlying Chlamydia infection is key.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive skin thickening starting from her fingers (sclerodactyly), telangiectasias, and dysphagia. Her face has a beaked nose and microstomia. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. Which of the following visceral complications is she LEAST likely to develop?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc), also known as CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias). Pulmonary hypertension is the leading cause of death in lcSSc. Pulmonary fibrosis can occur but is less common than in diffuse SSc. Scleroderma renal crisis (hypertension, oliguric renal failure) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and anti-RNA polymerase III antibodies — it is uncommon in lcSSc/CREST.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy presents with generalized blistering since birth, worsening with minor trauma. Blisters arise on palms, soles, and areas of friction. Nikolsky sign is positive. His older sibling has the same condition. Electron microscopy shows cytolysis within the basal keratinocyte layer. What is the inheritance pattern?
questions.exp: The clinical picture and ultrastructure (cytolysis within basal keratinocyte — suprabasal cleavage within the epidermis) is consistent with Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex (EBS) Weber-Cockayne or Dowling-Meara type. EBS is caused by mutations in keratin 5 (KRT5) or keratin 14 (KRT14) genes and is typically autosomal dominant. The Dowling-Meara variant is the most severe dominant form. Autosomal recessive EBS (due to plectin mutations) causes EBS with muscular dystrophy.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a verrucous plaque on his right hand for 2 years. He is a vegetable gardener. Culture shows a dimorphic fungus that grows as mycelium at 25°C (showing conidia arranged in a daisy-head pattern) and as yeast at 37°C. What is the MOST common route of infection?
questions.exp: This is sporotrichosis caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus. The characteristic form at 25°C is the 'daisy-head' arrangement of conidia on conidiophores. Infection typically occurs via traumatic inoculation of plant material (thorns of roses, sphagnum moss, barberry). The most common presentation is the lymphocutaneous form (sporotrichoid pattern). Fixed cutaneous sporotrichosis stays localized to site of inoculation. Inhalation causing pulmonary sporotrichosis is rare.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with a 2-cm painless firm nodule on his thigh. Excision biopsy shows spindle cells in a storiform pattern with occasional giant cells, hemosiderin deposits, and foamy macrophages. CD34 is positive on immunohistochemistry. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate management?
opts: Wide local excision with 2–3 cm margins
questions.exp: The histological features — storiform pattern, CD34 positivity, and foam cells — are consistent with Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP). DFSP is a locally aggressive fibrohistiocytic tumour with very low metastatic potential but high local recurrence rate. Wide local excision with 2–3 cm margins is the standard treatment. Mohs surgery is increasingly preferred in anatomically sensitive areas (face) as it offers equivalent control with tissue conservation. Imatinib is used for unresectable/metastatic DFSP (targets COL1A1-PDGFB fusion gene).

questions.q: A 68-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for RA presents with bilateral slate-grey discoloration of her shins and feet. Skin biopsy shows drug-melanin complexes in macrophages and melanocytes. Which melanin pathway is predominantly affected in antimalarial-induced pigmentation?
opts: Drug chelation with existing melanin causing colour change
questions.exp: Antimalarials (chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine) can cause drug-induced hyperpigmentation via chelation — they bind to melanin already present in melanosomes, forming drug-melanin complexes that are dark and cannot be metabolised. The resulting pigmentation is blue-grey to slate-grey and affects sun-exposed and pretibial areas particularly. Other mechanisms include iron chelation causing haemosiderin deposition. The pigmentation may partially fade after drug discontinuation.

questions.q: A 30-year-old man presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in the L2 dermatome distribution. He is HIV positive with CD4 count of 150 cells/μL. He had chickenpox at age 5. He develops new vesicles on the contralateral side 3 days later. What is this complication called and what is the appropriate antiviral duration?
opts: Bilateral zoster — treat for 7 days with acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day
Disseminated zoster — treat for 7–10 days with IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours
Zoster multiplex — treat for 5 days with valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS
Eczema herpeticum — treat for 10 days with acyclovir 400 mg TDS
questions.exp: Disseminated herpes zoster is defined as more than 20 vesicles outside the primary and adjacent dermatomes, or involvement of non-contiguous dermatomes. It occurs in immunocompromised individuals (HIV, transplants, malignancy). Treatment is IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours for 7–10 days (or until no new lesions for 48 hours), followed by oral therapy. Oral antivirals are inadequate for disseminated zoster. Ophthalmic involvement, visceral dissemination, and encephalitis must be monitored.

questions.q: A new-born presents with areas of absent skin (aplasia cutis congenita) over the scalp vertex at birth. Which of the following syndromes is MOST commonly associated with aplasia cutis congenita when there are also associated limb anomalies?
questions.exp: Adams-Oliver syndrome is characterized by aplasia cutis congenita (ACC) of the scalp and transverse limb defects (terminal limb reduction defects). It can be autosomal dominant (ARHGAP31, DOCK6 mutations) or autosomal recessive. Bart syndrome features ACC with junctional EB and nail dysplasia. Goltz syndrome (focal dermal hypoplasia) features skin atrophy/telangiectasias/fat herniation with skeletal anomalies — caused by PORCN gene mutations, X-linked dominant. Johanson-Blizzard syndrome features nasal alar aplasia, pancreatic insufficiency, and other anomalies.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with symmetrical thickening of the ear lobes and eyebrows (madarosis), diffuse skin infiltration, and a leonine facies. Slit-skin smear shows a bacterial index (BI) of 5+ and morphological index (MI) of 3%. Which observation from the MI is clinically significant?
opts: MI of 3% suggests treatment resistance since viable bacilli should be 0% after 3 months
MI of 3% means the disease is bacteriologically cured
MI of 3% suggests the patient is highly infectious
MI reflects antibiotic penetration into granulomas
questions.exp: The Morphological Index (MI) measures the percentage of viable (solid-staining) bacilli. In untreated lepromatous leprosy, MI can be 5–30%. Within 3 months of starting MDT, MI should fall to 0% (solid-staining bacilli become granular/fragmented as they die). An MI >0% after 3 months of adequate MDT suggests drug resistance or poor compliance. BI (bacterial index) remains elevated for years even after successful treatment as it counts both dead and live bacilli.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers (>3 times/year), genital ulcers, erythema nodosum-like lesions, and a positive pathergy test. Eye examination reveals hypopyon uveitis. Which HLA type is most strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: This is Behçet's disease (BD), a systemic vasculitis characterized by the classic triad of recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis (hypopyon uveitis is pathognomonic). Other features include erythema nodosum, positive pathergy test, and thrombophlebitis. HLA-B51 is most strongly associated with BD, particularly in populations along the Silk Road (Turkey, Iran, Japan). HLA-B27 is associated with reactive arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. Pathergy test: pustule at skin prick site after 24–48 hours.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a poorly-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma on her right cheek. Which of the following principles is the MAIN advantage of Mohs surgery over standard excision?
opts: Higher cure rates due to chemotherapy combined with surgery
Complete peripheral and deep margin examination allowing tissue conservation
Better cosmetic outcome due to primary closure technique
Reduced surgical time with equivalent cure rates
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) involves serial horizontal sectioning and immediate frozen section examination of 100% of the surgical margin (peripheral and deep), allowing precise removal of tumour while maximizing tissue conservation. Standard excision examines only bread-loafed vertical sections (examining <1% of margins). MMS has highest cure rates for BCC and SCC (>99% for primary BCC). It is indicated for high-risk tumours, recurrent tumours, and anatomically sensitive locations (face, genitalia).

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss 3 months after delivering her baby. Hair pull test shows 40 hairs with club/telogen roots. The scalp is normal. What is the CORRECT statement about this condition?
opts: The condition is caused by androgenetic changes post-partum
It results from synchronization of hair follicles into telogen phase triggered by physiological stress
Minoxidil 5% is required to prevent permanent hair loss
Scalp biopsy shows fibrous tract remnants indicating scarring alopecia
questions.exp: Post-partum telogen effluvium occurs 2–4 months after delivery. During pregnancy, elevated estrogens prolong the anagen (growth) phase, reducing normal shedding. After delivery, estrogen drops sharply, causing synchronous shift of many follicles to telogen. The condition is self-limiting — hair regrows fully within 6–12 months. No specific treatment is required. Scalp biopsy shows increased telogen:anagen ratio (>20% telogen) without scarring. It must be differentiated from female pattern hair loss (androgenetic) which is progressive.

questions.q: A 55-year-old immunosuppressed patient on tacrolimus post-renal transplant develops multiple verrucous papules on sun-exposed areas. HPV DNA typing reveals HPV types 5 and 8. What is the UNDERLYING condition that predisposes to this finding and the associated risk?
opts: Common warts due to HPV 6/11 — low risk of malignant transformation
Epidermodysplasia verruciformis-like lesions — risk of squamous cell carcinoma
Plane warts due to HPV 3/10 — risk of condylomata
Focal epithelial hyperplasia due to HPV 13/32 — benign condition
questions.exp: Epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV) is caused by mutations in EVER1/EVER2 genes leading to defective T-cell immunity against specific HPV types (5, 8, 9, 12, 14). EV-like lesions also occur in immunosuppressed individuals (HIV, organ transplant recipients). Beta-HPV types 5 and 8 are high-risk oncogenic types in EV/EV-like conditions, with 30–50% risk of squamous cell carcinoma on sun-exposed skin. Sun protection, retinoids, and imiquimod are used for management. HPV 6/11 cause condylomata (low risk); HPV 16/18 cause cervical/anogenital cancers.

questions.q: A 38-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of pruritic, papulovesicular eruption on the elbows, knees, scalp, and buttocks. It is intensely pruritic at night. Jejunal biopsy shows subtotal villous atrophy. Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits at the dermal papilla tips. What is the MOST important dietary advice?
opts: Low-fat diet to reduce cutaneous inflammation
Gluten-free diet as it treats both skin and intestinal disease
High-protein diet to compensate for intestinal losses
Dairy-free diet to reduce IgA-mediated allergy
questions.exp: This is Dermatitis Herpetiformis (DH), the cutaneous manifestation of coeliac disease. DH is characterized by intensely pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces, granular IgA at dermoepidermal junction (dermo-papillary tips), and gluten-sensitive enteropathy. A strict life-long gluten-free diet is the cornerstone of treatment — it improves both the skin disease and the enteropathy, and reduces the risk of intestinal lymphoma. Dapsone provides rapid symptomatic relief but does not treat the underlying gluten sensitivity. Dapsone can be slowly withdrawn once on GFD.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing pigmented lesion on his acral skin. Dermoscopy shows a parallel ridge pattern and irregular diffuse pigmentation. Histology reveals large epithelioid melanocytes with prominent nucleoli in the dermis with no junctional component in the epidermis. What stage does this histological finding suggest?
opts: Nodular melanoma — vertical growth phase without radial growth phase
questions.exp: Nodular melanoma (NM) is characterized histologically by vertical growth phase without a radial (horizontal) growth phase — there is no junctional component or pagetoid spread beyond the dermal tumour. NM grows rapidly and presents as a de novo thick pigmented or amelanotic nodule. It accounts for 15% of melanomas but is disproportionately responsible for melanoma deaths due to its rapid vertical invasion. Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) on acral skin shows parallel ridge pattern on dermoscopy and does have a junctional component.

questions.q: A 14-year-old girl presents with comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodules on her face, chest, and back for 2 years. After 6 months of oral doxycycline and topical tretinoin, she has persistent nodulo-cystic acne and scarring. The dermatologist starts her on isotretinoin. Which monitoring parameter is MOST critical before each prescription refill?
opts: Liver function tests and lipid profile
Serum zinc and vitamin A levels
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (category X). iPLEDGE (USA) / similar programmes mandate pregnancy testing before each monthly prescription. In female patients of childbearing potential: two forms of contraception are required, a negative pregnancy test before initiation, and monthly negative tests before each refill. LFTs and fasting lipids (triglycerides) are also monitored but the critical parameter that must be checked every month before prescribing is the pregnancy test in women. CBC monitoring is not routinely required.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with HIV (CD4: 200) presents with multiple, non-tender, violaceous papules and nodules on her lower legs, hard palate, and face. The lesions are non-blanching and biopsy shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular spaces with extravasated RBCs, and HHV-8 positive cells. Which cytokine is MOST responsible for the proliferative component of this tumour?
questions.exp: This is AIDS-related Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) caused by HHV-8 (KSHV). HHV-8 encodes viral FLICE inhibitory protein (vFLIP), viral cyclin D, and KSHV-GPCR that upregulate VEGF production. VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) acting via VEGFR-2 (KDR/Flk-1) is the key angiogenic and proliferative driver in KS. This is why anti-VEGF therapy and thalidomide (which inhibits VEGF) are used in KS. IL-6 (including viral IL-6 encoded by HHV-8) also promotes KS cell survival via STAT3.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents for evaluation of livedo reticularis, recurrent DVT, and spontaneous abortion. On examination she has a fixed, blotchy violaceous mottling of her arms in a net-like pattern. Antiphospholipid antibodies are positive. Which of the following differentiates livedo racemosa from physiological livedo reticularis?
opts: Livedo racemosa is reversible on warming; livedo reticularis is fixed
Livedo racemosa shows irregular, broken circles; livedo reticularis shows regular, complete rings
Livedo racemosa only occurs on lower limbs
Livedo reticularis is associated with systemic disease; livedo racemosa is always benign
questions.exp: Physiological livedo reticularis shows regular, complete, symmetric rings (net pattern) that are reversible on warming — caused by normal vasomotor response to cold. Livedo racemosa shows irregular, broken (incomplete) circles/rings in an asymmetric distribution — it is fixed (not reversible on warming) and is a marker of underlying pathology (antiphospholipid syndrome, SLE, polyarteritis nodosa, atherosclerosis, hyperviscosity). Sneddon's syndrome combines livedo racemosa with cerebrovascular disease. The presence of broken rings is the key distinguishing feature.

questions.q: A 34-year-old male presents with a moist, cauliflower-like growth on the perianal skin for 3 months. He has unprotected receptive anal intercourse. Biopsy shows koilocytes and papillomatous epidermal hyperplasia. Which HPV types are responsible and what is the implication for screening?
opts: HPV 16/18 — high risk for anal SCC, annual anal Pap smear recommended
HPV 6/11 — low oncogenic risk, no cancer screening needed
HPV 5/8 — associated with EV-like lesions in immunocompromised
questions.exp: Anogenital warts (condylomata acuminata) are caused by HPV 6 and 11, which are low-risk HPV types with minimal oncogenic potential. They cause benign but highly contagious warts. High-risk HPV types (16, 18, 31, 33) cause anogenital dysplasia and carcinoma but do not typically cause condylomata. However, MSM (men who have sex with men), particularly HIV-positive individuals, are at increased risk for anal SCC from high-risk HPV — anal Pap smear / high-resolution anoscopy is recommended for HIV-positive MSM. The condylomata themselves are from low-risk types.

questions.q: A 50-year-old farmer from Bihar presents with painless swelling of the foot with multiple sinuses draining black granules for 5 years. X-ray shows 'soap bubble' appearance of metatarsal bones. What organism is MOST likely causing this eumycetoma with black grains?
questions.exp: Mycetoma ('Madura foot') presents as a triad of tumefaction, sinuses, and grains. Eumycetoma (fungal) causes larger, firm grains. Madurella mycetomatis is the most common cause of eumycetoma with black/dark grains in Asia and Africa. X-ray shows 'soap bubble' cavities in bone in eumycetoma (vs. 'mortar and pestle' in actinomycetoma). Actinomycetoma (bacterial) causes finer, softer grains — Nocardia and Actinomadura cause white/yellow grains. Treatment: eumycetoma — itraconazole; actinomycetoma — prolonged sulfonamides/co-trimoxazole.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy presents with ash-leaf macules on his trunk, shagreen patches on his lower back, periungual fibromas, and adenoma sebaceum on his face. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Fundoscopy reveals retinal astrocytomas. Which gene pathway underlies this neurocutaneous disorder?
opts: Activation of NF1 gene leading to uncontrolled Ras/MAPK signalling
Loss of TSC1/TSC2 tumour suppressor genes leading to mTOR pathway overactivation
Gain-of-function PTCH1 mutations activating Hedgehog pathway
Loss of VHL gene leading to HIF-1alpha overexpression
questions.exp: This is Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC), a neurocutaneous phakomatosis. The hallmarks are ash-leaf macules (hypomelanotic macules — best seen under Wood's lamp), shagreen patches (connective tissue naevus), adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas), periungual fibromas (Koenen tumours), and cortical tubers causing epilepsy. TSC is caused by mutations in TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) genes, which are tumour suppressors that normally inhibit mTOR. Loss → mTOR overactivation → hamartoma growth. Everolimus (mTOR inhibitor) is used therapeutically. NF1 mutations cause neurofibromatosis type 1.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with erythematous, scaly plaques with a well-defined border and central clearing on his trunk. KOH mount of scales from the advancing border is negative for hyphae. However, punch biopsy shows psoriasiform hyperplasia, parakeratosis, and atypical lymphocytes in the epidermis forming Pautrier's microabscesses. What is the BEST initial treatment for early patch/plaque stage of this condition?
questions.exp: Pautrier's microabscesses with intraepidermal atypical lymphocytes are pathognomonic of Mycosis Fungoides (MF), the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CTCL). For early-stage MF (IA, IB — patch/plaque stage limited to skin), skin-directed therapies are first-line. Narrowband UVB is preferred for patch-stage MF (thinner lesions). PUVA is more effective for plaque stage and thicker lesions. Topical mechlorethamine (NM) and carmustine (BCNU) are also used for early MF. Oral bexarotene, vorinostat, and mogamulizumab are systemic agents for advanced/refractory MF.

questions.q: A 19-year-old woman with a history of atopic dermatitis presents with a widespread eruption of umbilicated vesicles coalescing into erosions 5 days after her partner was diagnosed with genital herpes. She has high-grade fever and lymphadenopathy. What is this complication called and what is the MOST important differentiating feature from severe atopic flare?
opts: Eczema herpeticum — monomorphic umbilicated vesicles/punched-out erosions vs. polymorphic atopic lesions
Kaposi varicelliform eruption — giant cells on Tzanck smear from lesion is diagnostic vs negative Tzanck in atopic flare
Both A and B refer to the same condition — HSV superinfection on eczematous skin
Generalized HSV — differentiated by positive HSV PCR on blood
questions.exp: Eczema herpeticum (EH) and Kaposi varicelliform eruption (KVE) are the same condition — disseminated HSV (usually HSV-1) infection in patients with atopic dermatitis or other skin barrier defects. It presents with monomorphic, umbilicated vesicles/pustules and punched-out erosions (unlike the polymorphic oozing lesions of atopic flare). Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells). Diagnosis confirmed by viral culture/PCR. Treatment is systemic acyclovir IV (severe) or oral (mild-moderate). FLG (filaggrin) mutations in atopic dermatitis impair skin barrier, predisposing to HSV dissemination.
